summary:
"Is it just me?" is a hunch fact-checker for the weather. You pick a place and a feeling, like "summers feel longer" or "frosts seem rarer", or type it in your own words. You make a guess first, then the app tests it against 45 years (1981–2025) of NASA POWER (MERRA-2) data.

It answers the Earth System Trend Detective challenge by running real trend tests (Mann-Kendall, Sen's slope and a 1,000-shuffle luck check). It covers 75 places, 49 UK towns and 26 world cities, and gives each hunch an honest verdict: real, not proven, not backed, or the opposite. The language model never calculates. It only matches your sentence to a result, so every number comes from NASA data.

It matters because climate change is easy to argue about and hard to feel. Starting from what people notice in their own town turns a trend test into a personal answer. In London, heatwave days rose from 7.2 a year in the 1980s to 18.7 in 2016–2025. The app also reports where the data say the feeling is wrong.
details:
Project Name
Is it just me?

High-Level Project Summary
Everyone has a feeling about the weather. Summers feel longer, nights feel warmer, frosts seem rarer. "Is it just me?" fact-checks those feelings. You pick a place and a hunch, or type it in your own words, and make a guess first. Then you see what 45 years of NASA POWER (MERRA-2) data say. Every hunch gets an honest verdict (real, signs of it but not proven, not backed, or the opposite). It also gets the size of the change, a luck test and a note on what the data can't tell you. It covers 75 places (49 UK towns, one per NASA grid square, and 26 world cities) and 1,142 tested trends. Climate change is easy to argue about and hard to feel. Starting from something people already notice in their own town turns a trend test into a personal answer. In London, heatwave days went from 7.2 a year in the 1980s to 18.7 in 2016–2025.

Link to Project Demo
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SAm_2GB7PGc

Link to Final Project
https://mostly-significant.vercel.app

Project Links (repo)
https://github.com/NaveenHerath/Mostly-Significant

Detailed Project Description

What it does

  • Say it your way: Type a hunch like "nights are unbearable in Manchester". The chat picks the place and the measure, asks for your guess, then shows a case card. If you ask about something the data can't test (snow, fog, a forecast), it says why and suggests related questions it can answer.
  • Pick a preset: Choose a place and a hunch, guess first, then see the verdict, the 1980s vs recent averages, the change per decade and a luck score.
  • The evidence: A chart of every year 1981–2025 with the trend line, and a grid of 1,000 shuffles showing how often chance alone beats the real trend.
  • Everywhere and Watch it change: Maps colouring every place by its verdict, and a year slider comparing each place with its own 1981–2010 normal.
  • Test your gut: An odd-one-out game (three nearby places, one went the other way) and a "Real, error or grid effect?" quiz on extreme moments in the data, such as Storm Eunice, the Singapore rain fault and London's 2022 heat. A gut score tracks your guesses and can be shared.

How it works
A Python pipeline downloads daily data for each place from the NASA POWER API. It runs a sea test so coastal cities use a land square, checks the data, and turns it into one number per year for each of 20 measures (18 per UK town, 10 per world city). Examples are heatwave days, warm nights, first frost, muggy nights, windy days and dry soil days. Each series is tested with the Mann-Kendall trend test (Hamed-Rao version for years that depend on each other), sized with Sen's slope, and checked with a luck test that shuffles the years 1,000 times. A verdict is "real" only when the trend is statistically significant (p < 0.05) and the direction matches the hunch. The website reads these precomputed results and calculates nothing itself.

The chat rule
The language model translates and explains, and never calculates. Gemini, or a small model in your browser, only picks a place and a measure from fixed lists. Every number comes from the results files. On 62 test questions both models picked the right test every time. Both were tuned on earlier misses from this set, so new sentences may do slightly worse.

Tools
Python (pandas, SciPy, pymannkendall), NASA POWER API, a static JavaScript site on Vercel, Gemini, and transformers.js for the on-device model.

Benefits and what we hope to achieve
It meets people where they are: their own hunch and their own town, not a climate report. It is honest when the data says "not backed" or "the opposite" (Plymouth's summer dry spells got shorter, 15.3 to 11.7 days), so people can trust the answers that come back real. We also flag 41 results that are weaker than they look.

Limitations
Values are averages over a roughly 50 km grid square, so local peaks read low. Sunshine data start in 1984. Trends are valid, but single-day extremes are understated.

I added the Limitations block because Validity is scored and the other sections don't state them. Delete it if the form has a length cap.
